Content:
Suppose that [MATH: a_n] is a sequence defined for [MATH: n\geq 1.] We know that the limit of a sequence (if it exists) is the unique number [MATH: L] such that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L.]

Content:
Intuitively, this statement means that the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: L] can be as small as we want, provided that [MATH: n] is large enough.

Content:
While intuition is important, none of this is very precise. What does "the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: L] can be as small as we want" mean? And what about "provided that [MATH: n] is large enough"? Can we quantify these ideas more precisely?

Content:
We need a precise mathematical definition of what's meant by the limit of a sequence. This lesson aims to construct a suitable definition in the case where [MATH: L=0.]

Content:
We start with a definition.

Content:
> A null sequence is a sequence that converges to zero.

Content:
For example, the sequence

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{1+n^2}, \qquad n\geq 1]
is a null sequence since
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((1)/(1 + n^{2})) = 0.]

Content:
On the other hand, the sequence
[MATH: b_n = n+1, \qquad n\geq 1]
is not a null sequence since
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)b_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)(n + 1); = ∞; ≠ 0.]

items.title: Identifying Null Sequences

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following are null sequences for [MATH: n\geq 1?]

  1. [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{n^2 + 1}]

  2. [MATH: b_n = \sqrt{n+1}]

  3. [MATH: c_n =\left(\dfrac89\right)^n]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following are null sequences for [MATH: n\geq 1?]

1. [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{n^2 + 1}]
2. [MATH: b_n = \sqrt{n+1}]
3. [MATH: c_n =\left(\dfrac89\right)^n]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A null sequence is a sequence that converges to zero:

  • Sequence I is a null sequence. By dividing the numerator and denominator by [MATH: n^2,] we have [MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((n)/(n^{2} + 1)); = lim_(n → ∞)((((n)/(n^{2})))/(((n^{2})/(n^{2}) + (1)/(n^{2})))); = lim_(n → ∞)((((1)/(n)))/((1 + (1)/(n^{2})))); = (0)/(1 + 0); = 0✓]

  • Sequence II is not a null sequence since [MATH: lim_(n → ∞)b_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)sqrt(n + 1); = ∞; ≠ 0.×]

  • Sequence III is null. Notice that this is a geometric sequence with the common ratio [MATH: r =\dfrac{8}{9}.] Since [MATH: |r| < 1,] the sequence converges to zero: [MATH: lim_(n → ∞)c_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((8)/(9))^{n}; = 0✓]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

items.title: Finding N Given a Concrete Epsilon

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the (null) geometric sequence [MATH: a_n,] defined by [MATH: a_n = \left(\dfrac23\right)^n, \qquad n\geq 1.]

Find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that [MATH: \left| a_n \right| < 0.000\,4] for all [MATH: n \geq N.]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the (null) geometric sequence [MATH: a_n,] defined by
[MATH: a_n = \left(\dfrac23\right)^n, \qquad n\geq 1.]

Find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that [MATH: \left| a_n \right| < 0.000\,4] for all [MATH: n \geq N.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We need to find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that

[MATH: \left| \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \right| < 0.000\,4]

for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

First, notice that [MATH: \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \gt 0] for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1.] With that in mind, we have

[MATH: \left|\left(\dfrac23\right)^n\right| = \left(\dfrac23\right)^n.]

Now, we solve the following inequality for [MATH: n]:

[MATH: ((2)/(3))^{n}|< 0.0004; \ln ((2)/(3))^{n}|< \ln (0.0004); n\ln ((2)/(3))|< \ln (0.0004); n|> (\ln (0.0004))/(\ln ((2)/(3))) = 19.296...]

As a result, [MATH: \left| \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \right| < 0.000\,4] for all natural numbers [MATH: n \geq \lceil19.296... \rceil =20.]

Therefore, [MATH: {\color{blue}{N}} ={\color{blue}{20}}.]

Content:

Content:
Let's calculate a few terms of the sequence to understand concretely what this result means:

Content:
- We expect that for [MATH: a_n] is larger than [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.000\, 4] when [MATH: n={\color{red}{19}}.] Indeed,
[MATH: a_{\color{red}{19}} = \left(\dfrac23\right)^{\color{red}{19}} \approx 0.000\,451 > \varepsilon.]
- However, for all [MATH: n\geq {\color{blue}{N}} ={\color{blue}{20}},] we have that [MATH: |a_n|] is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.000\,4{:}]
[MATH: a_{20}|= ((2)/(3))^{20} ≈ 0.000301 < ε✓; a_{21}|= ((2)/(3))^{21} ≈ 0.000200 < ε✓; a_{22}|= ((2)/(3))^{22} ≈ 0.000134 < ε✓; a_{23}|= ((2)/(3))^{23} ≈ 0.000089 < ε✓; ⋮]

Content:
The smallest value of [MATH: N] such that [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N] entirely depends on which value of [MATH: \varepsilon] we select.

Content:
For example, if we selected [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.000\,1,] then we'd need a larger value of [MATH: N] to satisfy [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.] We can see from the above calculations that we would select [MATH: {\color{purple}{N}}={\color{purple}{23}}.] Indeed:

Content:
[MATH: a_{22}|= ((2)/(3))^{22} ≈ 0.000134 > ε×; a_{23}|= ((2)/(3))^{23} ≈ 0.000089 < ε✓; a_{24}|= ((2)/(3))^{24} ≈ 0.000059 < ε✓; a_{24}|= ((2)/(3))^{25} ≈ 0.000040 < ε✓; ⋮]

Content:
Thus, the defining feature of a null sequence is that no matter how small [MATH: \varepsilon] is, we can always find an [MATH: N] such that [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: N] always depends on [MATH: \varepsilon,] we should think of [MATH: N] as a function of [MATH: \varepsilon,] i.e.,
[MATH: N= N(\varepsilon)]
We won't always write this explicitly, but you should keep this idea firmly in mind.

Content:
Proving that a given sequence is null relies on finding [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] for a given sequence. We'll return to this in future lessons.

Content:
Based on what we've discussed so far, the notation
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0]
means that if we take any arbitrarily small positive number [MATH: \varepsilon,] the distance of each [MATH: a_n] from zero is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for sufficiently large [MATH: n.]

Content:
This gives us our definition of a null sequence:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| a_n \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0e79625609c2d9d36d4a8d9114a68436]

Content:
For example, the statement

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right) = 0]
means the following:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
This definition is still informal. We can turn this into more formal language by explicitly including an implication:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that, for every natural number [MATH: n,] if [MATH: n \geq N,] then [MATH: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
Finally, by expressing the last statement using formal symbolic notation, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: a_n] is a sequence defined for [MATH: n\geq 1.] We know that the limit of a sequence (if it exists) is the unique number [MATH: L] such that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L.]

Content:
Intuitively, this statement means that the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: L] can be as small as we want, provided that [MATH: n] is large enough.

Content:
While intuition is important, none of this is very precise. What does "the distance between [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: L] can be as small as we want" mean? And what about "provided that [MATH: n] is large enough"? Can we quantify these ideas more precisely?

Content:
We need a precise mathematical definition of what's meant by the limit of a sequence. This lesson aims to construct a suitable definition in the case where [MATH: L=0.]

Content:
We start with a definition.

Content:
> A null sequence is a sequence that converges to zero.

Content:
For example, the sequence

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{1+n^2}, \qquad n\geq 1]
is a null sequence since
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((1)/(1 + n^{2})) = 0.]

Content:
On the other hand, the sequence
[MATH: b_n = n+1, \qquad n\geq 1]
is not a null sequence since
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)b_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)(n + 1); = ∞; ≠ 0.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Null Sequences

Example Prompt:
Which of the following are null sequences for [MATH: n\geq 1?]

1. [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{n^2 + 1}]
2. [MATH: b_n = \sqrt{n+1}]
3. [MATH: c_n =\left(\dfrac89\right)^n]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A null sequence is a sequence that converges to zero:

- Sequence I is a null sequence. By dividing the numerator and denominator by [MATH: n^2,] we have
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)a_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((n)/(n^{2} + 1)); = lim_(n → ∞)((((n)/(n^{2})))/(((n^{2})/(n^{2}) + (1)/(n^{2})))); = lim_(n → ∞)((((1)/(n)))/((1 + (1)/(n^{2})))); = (0)/(1 + 0); = 0✓]

- Sequence II is not a null sequence since
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)b_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)sqrt(n + 1); = ∞; ≠ 0.×]
- Sequence III is null. Notice that this is a geometric sequence with the common ratio [MATH: r =\dfrac{8}{9}.]
Since [MATH: |r| < 1,] the sequence converges to zero:
[MATH: lim_(n → ∞)c_{n}|= lim_(n → ∞)((8)/(9))^{n}; = 0✓]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Finding an Index Whose Subsequent Terms Are Close to Zero

Content:
Consider the following sequence:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{n}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
This is a null sequence since

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty} \left(\dfrac1n\right) = 0.]

Content:
Our intuitive understanding of this result tells us, "the distance between [MATH: a_n] and zero can be as small as we want, provided that [MATH: n] is large enough."

Content:
To make this idea more precise, we define a (small) positive real number [MATH: \varepsilon.] We're interested in the values of [MATH: n] such that the terms of the sequence all lie at a distance from zero that's smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon.] We express this as the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon]

Content:
Let's discuss the meaning of this inequality for some concrete values of [MATH: \varepsilon.]

Content:
- If [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.5,] then [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n \geq 3.] These values of [MATH: a_n] are those lying inside the yellow region below (from [MATH: n=3] onwards).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f6eac3f6526d27b4a9b63e97ae7e2020]

Content:
- If [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.3,] then [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n \geq 4.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/14df6198308319ea37b0cbe030082582]

Content:
- If [MATH: \varepsilon = 0.1,] then [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n \geq 11.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d3ea94d085a4806deaed0f1a00092510]

Content:
By making [MATH: \varepsilon] smaller and smaller, we can always find an index [MATH: N] where the distance between [MATH: a_n] and zero is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.] This is the critical property of a null sequence that we'll use to construct our precise definition.

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding N Given a Concrete Epsilon

Example Prompt:
Consider the (null) geometric sequence [MATH: a_n,] defined by
[MATH: a_n = \left(\dfrac23\right)^n, \qquad n\geq 1.]

Find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that [MATH: \left| a_n \right| < 0.000\,4] for all [MATH: n \geq N.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We need to find the smallest natural number [MATH: N] such that

[MATH: \left| \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \right| < 0.000\,4]

for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

First, notice that [MATH: \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \gt 0] for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1.] With that in mind, we have

[MATH: \left|\left(\dfrac23\right)^n\right| = \left(\dfrac23\right)^n.]

Now, we solve the following inequality for [MATH: n]:

[MATH: ((2)/(3))^{n}|< 0.0004; \ln ((2)/(3))^{n}|< \ln (0.0004); n\ln ((2)/(3))|< \ln (0.0004); n|> (\ln (0.0004))/(\ln ((2)/(3))) = 19.296...]

As a result, [MATH: \left| \left(\dfrac23\right)^n \right| < 0.000\,4] for all natural numbers [MATH: n \geq \lceil19.296... \rceil =20.]

Therefore, [MATH: {\color{blue}{N}} ={\color{blue}{20}}.]

Let's consider the null geometric sequence

[MATH: a_{22}|= ((2)/(3))^{22} ≈ 0.000134 > ε×; a_{23}|= ((2)/(3))^{23} ≈ 0.000089 < ε✓; a_{24}|= ((2)/(3))^{24} ≈ 0.000059 < ε✓; a_{24}|= ((2)/(3))^{25} ≈ 0.000040 < ε✓; ⋮]

Thus, the defining feature of a null sequence is that no matter how small [MATH: \varepsilon] is, we can always find an [MATH: N] such that [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Definition of the Limit of a Null Sequence

Content:
Based on what we've discussed so far, the notation
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0]
means that if we take any arbitrarily small positive number [MATH: \varepsilon,] the distance of each [MATH: a_n] from zero is smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] for sufficiently large [MATH: n.]

Content:
This gives us our definition of a null sequence:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| a_n \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
For example, the statement

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right) = 0]
means the following:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
This definition is still informal. We can turn this into more formal language by explicitly including an implication:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that, for every natural number [MATH: n,] if [MATH: n \geq N,] then [MATH: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
Finally, by expressing the last statement using formal symbolic notation, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{1}{n} \right| \lt \varepsilon]
